questions.q: Define positive health according to the NCERT textbook and list its five constructs.
questions.a: Positive health is a state of complete physical, mental, social, and spiritual well-being, not merely the absence of disease. Its five constructs are: (1) a healthy body, (2) high quality of personal relationships, (3) a sense of purpose in life, (4) self-regard and mastery of life's tasks, and (5) resilience to stress, trauma, and change. A wrong answer that equates positive health with "absence of illness" reveals a biomedical rather than holistic understanding, missing the proactive, asset-based nature of the concept.

questions.q: Explain the difference between "social network" and "perceived social support" and why only the latter correlates with well-being.
questions.a: Social network refers to the quantity of social connections (number of people), while perceived social support refers to the quality — the subjective belief that one is cared for, valued, and can rely on others. Only perceived support correlates with well-being because a large network without emotional closeness is time-consuming to maintain and may not provide actual comfort during stress. A student who confuses the two may think "having many Facebook friends" buffers stress, revealing a misunderstanding of the functional vs. structural distinction.

questions.q: A student facing board exams reports: "I eat junk food, don't exercise, think I'll fail, and avoid friends." Using the five pillars of positive health, design a 4-week intervention plan with one specific, measurable action per pillar per week.
questions.a: Week 1: Diet — replace one junk meal/day with a fruit + nut snack; Exercise — 15-min walk 3×/week; Attitude — write one realistic appraisal of exam preparedness daily; Optimism — note one study success each evening; Support — message one friend for 10-min chat. Week 2: Increase walk to 20-min 4×/week; add protein to breakfast; challenge one catastrophic thought; visualize handling a tough question; study with a peer once. Week 3: Meal-prep two healthy lunches; add stretching; reframe "I'll fail" to "I'm preparing"; share a worry with a parent; join a study group. Week 4: Sustain all; add one strength exercise; teach a concept to a friend (mastery); mentor a junior (purpose). A plan lacking specificity (e.g., "eat better") reveals inability to operationalize abstract pillars.

questions.q: Compare and contrast Kobasa's three Cs of hardiness (commitment, control, challenge) with the three resources of resilience (I HAVE, I AM, I CAN). Which framework is more actionable for a stressed adolescent and why?
questions.a: Hardiness describes enduring personality traits: commitment (engagement vs. alienation), control (influence vs. helplessness), challenge (growth vs. threat). Resilience resources are developmental assets: I HAVE (external supports), I AM (internal strengths), I CAN (skills). Hardiness is trait-like; resilience resources are buildable. For an adolescent, resilience is more actionable because "I CAN learn problem-solving" is a concrete skill target, whereas "develop control" is vague. A student who says "they're the same" misses the trait vs. resource distinction and the developmental implication.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "Optimism is always adaptive because it reduces stress." Use evidence from the NCERT text on coping styles of optimists vs. pessimists.
questions.a: The statement is partially false. Optimism is adaptive when it fuels problem-focused coping (planning, seeking advice) but maladaptive if it becomes unrealistic optimism (ignoring risks, denying stress). NCERT notes optimists use more problem-focused strategies and seek help; pessimists use avoidance/denial. However, "blind optimism" — e.g., "I don't need to study, it'll work out" — impairs preparation. A student who agrees uncritically misses the crucial distinction between realistic optimism (expecting favorable outcomes *with effort*) and Pollyanna optimism (expecting favorable outcomes *without effort*).

questions.q: Create a "Positive Health Audit" checklist for a residential school that assesses all five pillars + hardiness + resilience resources. Include 3 observable indicators per pillar that a warden could rate weekly.
questions.a: Diet: (1) % students eating breakfast daily, (2) variety score of mess menu (food groups/day), (3) junk food access frequency. Exercise: (1) min of moderate activity/day, (2) participation rate in sports/yoga, (3) screen-time <2hrs non-academic. Attitude: (1) % using "I can improve" language in reflections, (2) tolerance score in conflict resolution, (3) humor use in assemblies. Optimism: (1) future-goal specificity in journals, (2) help-seeking frequency, (3) reframing setbacks in counseling logs. Support: (1) trusted adult named, (2) peer confidant identified, (3) family contact frequency. Hardiness: (1) club/activity commitment (attendance), (2) self-rated control over schedule, (3) voluntary challenge uptake. Resilience: I HAVE — mentor assigned; I AM — self-esteem scale; I CAN — problem-solving demo. A checklist missing observables (e.g., "students feel supported") reveals confusion between internal states and measurable proxies.
